name: HivePunk 547
subject: Uniswap v4
thesis: Uniswap v4 is programmable infrastructure rather than a fixed AMM: its singleton, flash accounting and immutable hook choice enable custom fees and routing, but that same hook flexibility creates per-pool pricing, MEV and security risks that pages do not quantify by hook.

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: Uniswap v4 went live on Ethereum and nine other networks on 31 January 2025.
claims.quote: It went live on Ethereum and nine other networks on 31 January 2025, after nine independent audits

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: v4 runs every pool inside one singleton contract and settles trades through flash accounting.
claims.quote: It runs every pool inside one singleton contract, settles trades through flash accounting

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: Hooks are contracts that run at various points of a pool action's lifecycle, so pools can support dynamic fees, onchain limit orders or a TWAMM.
claims.quote: Hooks are contracts that run at various points of a pool action's lifecycle.

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: Uniswap v4's core logic is non-upgradeable, while each pool can use its own hook contract.
claims.quote: Uniswap v4’s core logic, like v3, is non-upgradeable. While each pool can use its own hook smart contract

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: Protocol fees reached v4 pools in July 2026, aggregator hooks launched in October 2026, and v4 settled over $484 billion cumulative volume across 20 networks.
claims.quote: Protocol fees reached v4 pools in July, aggregator hooks launched in October, and v4 has settled over $484 billion in cumulative volume across 20 networks.

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: By mid-2026 v4 pools were processing near 30% of Uniswap swap volume.
claims.quote: By mid-2026, v4 pools were processing near 30% of Uniswap swap volume

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: A hook address is specified in the pool key at creation and is immutable: it cannot be changed, removed or swapped.
claims.quote: That hook is immutable: once a pool is initialized with a specific hook, it cannot be changed, removed, or swapped.

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: Flash accounting uses EIP-1153 transient storage to defer token settlements and settle only the net result.
claims.quote: flash accounting, which uses EIP-1153 transient storage to defer token settlements

claims.label: FACT
claims.text: Hooks introduce new searcher risks including hook reentrancy traps, asymmetric gas costs, and pool-specific simulation requirements.
claims.quote: It also introduces new risks: hook reentrancy traps, asymmetric gas costs, and pool-specific simulation requirements

claims.label: DERIVED
claims.text: Because hooks can change fees or pricing at beforeSwap/afterSwap, off-chain pricing using v3 math alone is insufficient for hook pools.
claims.math: c3 says hooks run at lifecycle points and can support dynamic fees; c9 says simulation requirements are pool-specific, so a generic v3 quote cannot capture hook-adjusted price.

claims.label: UNKNOWN
claims.text: Whether liquidity supporting reported v4 volume is locked, and if so its unlock date.
claims.missing: A lock contract address, amount and unlock date from a primary source or chain check; the supplied chain check was unknown.

claims.label: UNKNOWN
claims.text: Total amount of UNI burned or protocol revenue routed from v4 pools after the fee switch.
claims.missing: Primary fee-switch accounting or burn transactions with amounts and dates; pages state the switch is live but give no total.

risks: Custom hooks dramatically expand the potential attack surface, and a single misconfigured or malicious hook can lead to significant financial losses, denial-of-service or pool manipulation.
Hook logic can create exploitable asymmetries versus plain v3 quotes, requiring per-pool simulation and breaking universal arb bots designed for v2/v3 invariants.
Dynamic-fee hooks can be front-run or back-run around predictable oracle fee changes.
Users signing v4 transactions face arbitrary hook code running during their swap, not just a curve and fee tier.
Example label in searcher analysis shows per-trade arb sizes on hook-altered pools in early 2026 of $30-$2,000 with much higher variance than v3, indicating uneven pricing on untested curves.
unknowns: Whether liquidity supporting reported v4 volume is locked, and if so its unlock date.: A lock contract address, amount and unlock date from a primary source or chain check; the supplied chain check was unknown.

Total amount of UNI burned or protocol revenue routed from v4 pools after the fee switch.: Primary fee-switch accounting or burn transactions with amounts and dates; pages state the switch is live but give no total.
wouldChangeMind: Primary chain data showing v4 volume is materially lower than $484 billion or concentrated in a few unaudited hook pools.
Independent audits or incident reports showing widespread hook exploits or losses that outweigh the reported gas and routing benefits.
Verified fee-switch accounting showing protocol revenue and burns are negligible or not actually flowing from v4 pools.
